claims.text: The material is an NbMoCrTiAl refractory high-entropy alloy composite produced by high-energy ball milling and spark plasma sintering.
The composite contains a BCC solid-solution matrix with approximately 32 vol.% TiC and 7 vol.% Al2O3.
The untreated composite has a room-temperature compressive fracture strength of approximately 1542 MPa.
The untreated composite exhibits cleavage-type fracture without appreciable room-temperature ductility.
The BCC matrix itself is predominantly brittle.
A post-sintering lower-temperature anneal can induce dispersed, sub-micron ductile precipitates in the BCC matrix.
The proposed lower-temperature anneal will relieve residual stresses.
The proposed precipitates will act as dislocation sources and promote plastic deformation.
The proposed precipitates will impede crack propagation.
A dual-phase microstructure containing a modified ductile matrix while retaining TiC and Al2O3 reinforcement will produce more uniform deformation under load.
Particle strengthening and grain refinement will preserve high strength after the heat treatment.
The heat treatment will significantly increase strain to failure and uniform deformability relative to the standard SPS baseline.
The heat treatment will improve impact energy absorption relative to the standard SPS baseline.
After heat treatment, compressive strength will remain within approximately 5–10% of the baseline value of 1542 MPa.
The heat treatment will preserve impact-induced energy release.
The baseline SPS densification is performed at high temperature.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls the intervention a post-sintering two-step heat treatment, but the intervention describes the first step as the already-used high-temperature densification/SPS operation followed by only one post-SPS annealing step. It is therefore unclear whether two additional post-sintering steps or SPS plus one anneal are proposed.
